chunks: I wrote to the man (peace be upon him) asking him that your followers had differed regarding the Knowledge. So some of them said, 'God did not cease to be a Knower before He did (created) the things'; and some of them said, 'We do not say that God did not cease to be a Knower, because the meaning of "He knows" is "He acts". So if we affirm the Knowledge (as eternal), then we have affirmed in the (pre-)eternity something along with Him'. So if you see fit — may God make me your ransom — that you teach me from that what I may stop at and not exceed.
So he (peace be upon him) wrote in his own handwriting: 'God did not cease to be a Knower. Blessed and Exalted is His Mention.'

key_terms.الْأَزَلُ: pre-eternity, eternity a parte ante — existence without beginning
key_terms.الْعِلْمُ: Knowledge — here specifically God's attribute of omniscience, its eternity being the theological question at stake
key_terms.بِخَطِّهِ: in his own handwriting — signifying the personal authenticity and deliberate weight of the Imam's response
key_terms.تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى ذِكْرُهُ: Blessed and Exalted is His Mention — a formula of glorification emphasizing God's transcendence beyond all human conceptual categories
key_terms.لَمْ يَزَلِ: a phrase meaning 'did not cease to be', used to express pre-eternal continuity — God was always X

ai.seo_question: Did God always have knowledge before creating things? What does the Imam teach about God's eternal pre-temporal knowledge in Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: This hadith records a written exchange between a follower and an Imam (referred to as 'the man', a protective epithet used during the Abbasid persecution to avoid openly naming the Imam) concerning a theological dispute within the Shi'a community about the eternality of God's knowledge. One group affirmed that God was always a Knower before creating anything; the other group hesitated, fearing that affirming eternal knowledge would imply the co-eternity of objects of knowledge alongside God, which would be tantamount to shirk. The Imam's brief but authoritative written response — 'God did not cease to be a Knower. Blessed and Exalted is His Mention' — definitively settles the dispute by affirming divine pre-eternal knowledge, while the closing glorification formula redirects focus to God's transcendence, indicating that His knowledge transcends the ordinary relational understanding of knowing.
